entries.topic: Who Walter Rothschild was: title, Parliament, the bank, Tring, money

claims.text: Lionel Walter Rothschild was born in London on 8 February 1868 and died at Tring on 27 August 1937.

He succeeded his father, Nathan ('Natty') Rothschild, 1st Baron Rothschild, in the peerage in 1915; Natty died in London on 31 March 1915, aged 74, after an operation. (The Rothschild Archive family page words this as 'five days after an operation on 31 March', which could put the death in early April; check against the Oxford DNB.)

He sat as MP for Aylesbury from 6 January 1899 until the January 1910 general election, when he retired. Wikipedia gives his party as Liberal Unionist (Conservative after 1912); the Jewish Virtual Library calls him a Conservative MP.

He worked at the family bank, N M Rothschild & Sons (New Court), from 1889 to 1908, and left it in 1908 to work on natural history. Wikipedia, citing his niece Miriam Rothschild's 2008 biography, says he 'evidently lacked any interest or ability' in finance (approximate quote).

His zoological museum at Tring opened to the public in 1892, on land his father gave him in 1889. He employed taxonomists Ernst Hartert and Karl Jordan, about 400 collectors in all, and started the journal Novitates Zoologicae in 1894. He left the museum and its collections to the British Museum; it is now the Natural History Museum at Tring.

In the early 1930s he sold most of his bird collection, about 280,000 specimens, to the American Museum of Natural History in New York. Popular accounts give the price as $225,000 and date the sale to 1931; Wikipedia says 1932. Leonard Sanford persuaded Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney and her children to buy it for the museum.

The reason for the sale is reported to be blackmail. His niece and biographer Miriam Rothschild revealed in Dear Lord Rothschild (1983) that a former mistress had blackmailed him for decades; she did not name the blackmailer. Wikipedia carries the blackmail claim with citations to Miriam Rothschild (1983) and Mark Barrow (2000).
No figure for Walter's estate at his death in 1937, or for Natty's estate in 1915, was found on any page fetched in this pass.

Wikipedia says he served as president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews from 1925 to 1926. The Times of Israel blog by former Board president Vivian Wineman calls him Senior Vice-President of the Board in 1917.

Whether Walter held office in the English Zionist Federation is disputed. Al Jazeera's Behind Balfour says he was its president, and Wineman calls him President of the Zionist Federation. A Wikipedia-derived page instead says Weizmann became president of the (British) Zionist Federation in 1917. The Rothschild Archive and Wikipedia's biography name no Zionist office for him.

He presented the original Balfour letter, with Hankey's covering letter of 6 October 1917 asking his views on the draft, to the British Library (then the British Museum Library) in 1924; it is Add MS 41178 A.

entries.topic: Why the letter went to Walter Rothschild, not Weizmann

claims.text: Balfour's letter of 2 November 1917 was addressed to Lord Rothschild at 148 Piccadilly and asked him to pass the declaration to the Zionist Federation.

The Rothschild Archive calls Walter the 'unofficial leader of the British Jewish community'. Jacob, 4th Lord Rothschild, writing in the Jewish Chronicle in 2017, says Walter inherited the title and the family's leadership of British Jewry from his father in 1915.

Jacob Rothschild quotes Nahum Sokolow as saying the Zionists 'had no address' while Walter had a very fine one at 148 Piccadilly (approximate quote), and says the historian Cecil Roth called the choice 'incongruous'.

Jewish News (2016) explains that the letter went to Rothschild rather than Weizmann because Weizmann 'was not the most senior member of the Zionist hierarchy', and Rothschild, as de facto head of the community, was to pass it to the Zionist Federation.
On 19 June 1917 Balfour asked Rothschild and Weizmann to submit a formula; Weizmann had written to the Foreign Office (Graham) on 13 June urging a public statement (Wikipedia, citing Friedman 1973).

The Zionist draft dated 12 July 1917 in Wikipedia's table of drafts, sent by Lord Rothschild to Balfour on 18 July, had two points. First, His Majesty's Government 'accepts the principle that Palestine should be reconstituted' as the national home of the Jewish people. Second, the government would use its best endeavours and discuss methods with the Zionist Organisation. The National Archives holds an item dated 18 July 1917, CAB 21/58 (222), catalogued as 'Balfour to Rothschild'.

Against the final text: 'accepts the principle' became 'view with favour'; 'reconstituted' was dropped and 'that Palestine' became 'in Palestine' (Milner's amendment); two safeguard clauses were added in early October, one for the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities and one for the status of Jews elsewhere (Stein 1961, via Wikipedia). Rothschild objected to the second clause as implying a danger to non-Zionists, which he denied (Ingram 2009, via Wikipedia).

Weizmann settled in Manchester in 1904 as a chemistry lecturer at the university and became the leading Zionist spokesman in Britain. His wartime acetone work brought him to senior officials, and he was appointed scientific adviser to the Ministry of Munitions in September 1915. Historians reject Lloyd George's 1932 claim that his meetings with Weizmann were the 'fount and origin' of the declaration.

Nahum Sokolow, a journalist and executive of the World Zionist Organization, moved to Britain in 1914, was received by Pope Benedict XV on 6 May 1917, and obtained the French Cambon letter of 4 June 1917 (Wikipedia).

Weizmann met Walter Rothschild in late 1914, introduced through Dorothy de Rothschild (Dunner) or through Walter's sister-in-law Rozsika (Jacob Rothschild). Weizmann wrote to Dorothy 33 times between 1914 and 1916.

entries.topic: The official British Jewish leadership against political Zionism, May–June 1917

claims.text: David Lindo Alexander was president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews from 1903 to 1917, and Claude Montefiore was president of the Anglo-Jewish Association. Together they ran the Conjoint Foreign Committee.

On 24 May 1917 The Times (p. 5, 'The Future of the Jews. Palestine and Zionism') published a statement signed by Alexander and Montefiore. It objected to treating the Jewish settlements in Palestine as national in a political sense, to special rights for Jewish settlers, and to a Jewish chartered company.

Wineman dates the letter to 25 May and names Lucien Wolf (spelled 'Woolf') and Alexander as signatories; Dunner says Wolf wrote it for the Conjoint Committee. Wikipedia and Grobman name Alexander and Montefiore.

Walter Rothschild replied in The Times, objecting that opponents, 'a mere fraction' of Jewish opinion, sought to interfere (Dunner, approximate quote). Dunner says the reply ran the next day; Wikipedia's sources list a Times piece of 28 May 1917, p. 5 ('The Future of the Jews. Zionist Projects'). No dated Weizmann reply in The Times was confirmed in this pass.
On 17 June 1917 the Board of Deputies passed a motion censuring the statement by 56 votes to 51. Alexander had treated it as a confidence vote and resigned; other honorary officers also resigned.
Alexander and Montefiore later took part in founding the anti-Zionist League of British Jews.
Wineman says the Foreign Office wrote to Weizmann and Lord Rothschild a day or so after the vote asking for proposals. This fits Wikipedia's date of 19 June for Balfour's request.
Natalie Livingstone writes that the English Rothschilds had earlier opposed Zionism as a threat to their work integrating Jews into British society.

claims.text: Edwin Montagu, the only Jewish member of the Cabinet (Secretary of State for India from 1917), submitted a memorandum dated 23 August 1917. The National Archives catalogues it as CAB 21/58 (218), 'Anti-Semitism in the Present Government'; the Jewish Virtual Library prints it as 'The Anti-Semitism of the Present Government'.

Montagu called Zionism a 'mischievous political creed' that no patriotic British citizen could hold, wrote 'I assert that there is not a Jewish nation', and warned that the policy would become 'a rallying ground for Anti-Semites' (short quotes from the JVL text).

He predicted that Jews would be 'treated as foreigners in every country but Palestine' and that 'Palestine will become the world's Ghetto'. He asked the government to 'go no further' (short quotes from the JVL text).
Grobman cites Martin Gilbert on Montagu's fears and records that Weizmann dismissed his opposition.

entries.topic: Test: was the declaration a quid pro quo for Rothschild money or war loans?

claims.text: No page fetched in this pass records a payment, loan or financial undertaking by Walter Rothschild or N M Rothschild & Sons in exchange for the declaration. Walter had left the bank in 1908.

Jonathan Schneer (2010) argues that British leaders courted an 'international Jewry' they wrongly believed powerful. In his account they relied on antisemitic canards: that Jews controlled US finance and could bring America into the war, and that Jews were behind Russian pacifism. He adds that they believed Jewish money could help finance the war. This is a claim about British officials' beliefs, not about any transaction.

Wikipedia, citing Schneer, quotes Robert Cecil as writing that he did not think it possible 'to exaggerate the international power of the Jews' (approximate quote). James Renton describes the foreign-policy elite's belief that Jews had real power that could be useful in the war.
The Rothschild Archive says that from 1916 the British hoped Jews would help finance the growing costs of the war. It gives no loan or sum linked to the declaration.

Yehuda Bauer and Moshe Fox (Jewish Chronicle, 2018) say the letter went to Walter because 'the Rothschilds were the perceived head of Jewish international financial power'. They present this as an antisemitic assumption by British officials, not as evidence of a financial deal.
Al Jazeera's Behind Balfour lists a wish to attract Jewish financial resources among the reasons Lloyd George's memoirs give. It reports no specific loan.

Natty's documented wartime help was advice to Lloyd George on steadying the currency in August 1914. He reportedly said 'Tax the rich, and tax them heavily' (Roth 1939, via Wikipedia). In 1915 he led a British Red Cross appeal to raise £1 million. Natty died in 1915, two and a half years before the declaration.

Overall: the claim that the declaration was bought with Rothschild money is not established by any source reached here. The documented finding, made by Schneer and by Bauer and Fox, is that British officials believed in an exaggerated Jewish financial and political power and hoped to win it over.

entries.topic: [Modern context] US step-up in basis at death, 26 U.S.C. §1014

claims.text: Under 26 U.S.C. §1014(a)(1), the basis of property acquired from a decedent is generally 'the fair market value of the property at the date of the decedent's death'.

Effect: any gain that built up during the decedent's life is never taxed as capital gain. In an illustrative example, a home bought for $35,000 and worth $100,000 at death takes a $100,000 basis, so selling it at $100,000 yields no taxable gain. Basis can also step down when value has fallen.

ProPublica (2021) describes 'buy, borrow, die', a phrase it attributes to USC tax law professor Edward McCaffery. The wealthy hold appreciating assets, borrow against them (loans are not income), and at death the gains escape capital-gains tax through the step-up in basis, which ProPublica says experts across the political spectrum see as a flaw.

claims.text: ProPublica (Jesse Eisinger, Jeff Ernsthausen and Paul Kiel, 8 June 2021) reported that the 25 richest Americans' wealth grew by a combined $401 billion from 2014 to 2018 (Forbes estimates), while they paid $13.6 billion in federal income tax (IRS data).
ProPublica called the ratio, 3.4%, the 'true tax rate'. It compares taxes paid with the estimated growth in wealth, not with taxable income; unrealized gains are not income under US tax law.

For contrast, ProPublica said the median American household earned about $70,000 a year and paid about 14% in federal taxes. That is a rate on income, so it does not compare directly with the 3.4% 'true tax rate'.

claims.text: For estates of people dying in 2026, the federal basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 per person, up from $13,990,000 for 2025 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32 and IRS release IR-2025-103, both 9 October 2025, as summarised by KPMG).

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act made the $15 million gift, estate and generation-skipping exemption permanent, with no sunset, and indexed for inflation in later years. The annual gift exclusion stays at $19,000 per recipient for 2026 (Morgan Lewis).

claims.text: On 6 February 2023 Rothschild & Co announced that the family holding company, Rothschild & Co Concordia, would tender for the shares it did not own and take the Paris-listed bank private. The offer was €48 per share, a 19% premium to the previous close of €40.25. Reuters valued the bank at about €3.6 billion.

Before the offer, Concordia held 38%, and the wider family held close to 55% of shares and 69% of voting rights at end-2022 (Reuters). The company's presentation gives the enlarged family concert as 54.5% of capital and 66.8% of voting rights. The group is led by Alexandre de Rothschild, son of David de Rothschild.
The €48 offer included distributions: a €1.4 ordinary dividend and an €8.0 exceptional distribution. The net squeeze-out price was €38.60 per share (48.0 − 9.4).
New members of the shareholder pact included the Wertheimer brothers (owners of Chanel) and the Peugeot and Dassault families (Reuters, 13 February 2023).

The squeeze-out and delisting from Euronext Paris took effect on 11 October 2023. Before it, the Concordia concert held 88.74% of capital (95.64% including assimilated shares) and at most 4,151,098 shares (5.37%) were squeezed out (AMF notice of 3 October 2023).

entries.topic: [Modern context] The Kushner-linked resort projects in Albania (Sazan, Zvërnec)

claims.text: In February 2024 Albania's parliament amended the law on protected areas to allow high-end tourism developments, including five-star hotels, in certain zones. In March 2024 Jared Kushner posted sketches for projects on Sazan Island and the Zvërnec coast. In December 2024 the government gave 'strategic investor' status to a Kushner-linked company (AFP).

Who is behind it. Al Jazeera and other outlets call it a project of Kushner's firm Affinity Partners. A spokesperson for Sazan Real Estate Development (registered in Qatar, October 2025) told Reuters that Kushner and others invested personally, not through Affinity; Reuters could not confirm this. Sazan confirms Kushner is an investor but has not disclosed the size of his stake. AFP reports that Asher Abehsera leads the company.

The Zvërnec site lies in the Vjosa-Narta protected area, a wetland with flamingos, seals and sea-turtle nesting (Reuters, Al Jazeera). OCCRP names it the Pishë-Poro-Nartë protected area. That name comes from an October 2022 Council of Ministers decision which, according to the BirdLife partner PPNEA, merged Vjosë-Nartë with Pishë Poro and removed 5,551.7 ha from protection, including the Vlora airport site.
Reported values differ: Sazan alone at about €1.4 billion (Al Jazeera), and the whole project at about $4 billion (OCCRP, The New Region).

On 21 November 2025 Artur Shehu agreed to sell Zvërnec land to Albania Land Development for an estimated €5.5 million. The sale was finalised on 26 April 2026 at a declared €122 million (AFP); Reuters gives about €110 million. Zvërnec residents won a 2013 court ruling on ownership; Shehu appealed, and the case is unresolved.

SPAK, the anti-corruption prosecutor, acted on or about 2 June 2026. It ordered a preventive seizure of Albania Land Development's bank accounts (OCCRP), and its probe concerns the funds behind the land titles and their sale (Al Jazeera). The New Region reports that it also investigated the 2024 legal reform.

SPAK case files dated 12 June 2026 allege that Shehu's network bought land with drug proceeds and forged documents, and arrest warrants were issued for 20 people. SPAK froze the roughly €110 million sale proceeds in a notary account. Shehu denies the allegations. The files make no allegation against Kushner, Sazan, Albania Land Development or the other investors (Reuters, 11 July 2026).

Protests, known as the 'Flamingo Revolution', began on 30 May 2026 over fencing and barbed wire at Zvërnec. Private guards injured protesters; one guard was charged and two security firms lost their licences. Thousands marched in Tirana in early June under the slogan 'Albania is not for sale'. Prime Minister Edi Rama said the investment would not stop while he is in office.

Status as of 11 August 2026, the latest reporting found: the funds remain frozen, and CBS reported that a court confirmed an order for more than $127 million. The government says the project is going ahead, and investors are reworking the masterplan. As of mid-June 2026 the fence had been removed and bulldozers had left the site. No report later than August 2026 was found.

Protothema (17 August 2026), citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that the sale funds remained frozen, that Shehu faces charges including money laundering and membership of a criminal organisation, which he denies, that the investor consortium says it is not under investigation, and that the project was in environmental assessment.
